[In this chapter, I show how to test for overreporting, and in @sec-deconvolution how to recover its distribution.]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}[In this section, I show how to test for overreporting and recover its distribution.]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"} @eq-share-net shows that the share of materials equals the output elasticity of materials and the output error. Importantly, under Cobb-Douglas, the output elasticity of materials is constant and does not depend on productivity. In general, the output elasticity of the flexible input of a Hicks-neutral production function does not depend on productivity conditional on inputs. This is what allows me to distinguish between overreporting and productivity.

Since corporations report materials truthfully and share a common technology with unincorporated firms, the output elasticity of materials can be recovered from corporations, even though corporations and unincorporated firms are heterogeneous in productivity. The difference between the materials share of gross output of unincorporated firms and the output elasticity of materials then recovers overreporting up to the output measurement error.

The difference forms an observed residual whose expected value can be tested. Under the null hypothesis of correct reporting, the expected value of this residual is zero. Under the alternative, it is positive.

The distribution of the unincorporated firms' residual is a convolution of the distributions of overreporting and measurement error, and can be used to recover the distribution of overreporting. Because the output measurement error is independent of juridical organization and corporations do not overreport, I can recover the distribution of the measurement error from the residual of corporations. Deconvolution requires the addends to be independent and the distribution of one of them to be known. Measurement error is independent of overreporting, and its distribution is known. It follows that the distribution of overreporting is identified.

The method can be applied to any dataset containing firm-level inputs and output, and a benchmark group. Firm-level surveys, administrative firm records, or confidential transaction-level invoice data usually contain both.

I find that among the 20 largest manufacturing industries in Colombia during the sample period, the test rejects correct reporting in 9 of the 18 industries liable for the sales tax and in neither exempt industry. In the 5 largest industries where the test rejects at the 1 percent level and the deconvolution applies, unincorporated firms overreport on average between 4.5 and 23.2 percent of their true materials.

## The reported materials share {#sec-testing-share}

Regardless of juridical organization, firms in an industry share the Cobb-Douglas technology of @eq-pf, $Y_{it}=M^{\beta}_{it}K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})$, but may differ in productivity. The econometrician observes output, capital, labour, and prices of intermediate inputs and output, and the sales-tax rates on sales and on purchases, $\{Y_{it},K_{it},L_{it},\rho_t,P_t,\tau_S,\tau_P\}$, but she only observes overreported intermediate inputs, $M^*_{it}=M_{it}+e_{it}$.

Let $s_{it}$ denote the log share of reported materials in output, net of sales taxes, $s_{it}\equiv\ln\big((1-\tau_P)\rho_tM^*_{it}/(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}\big)$.^[In the single-tax model (@sec-app-single-tax) the tax terms cancel and $s_{it}$ is the gross share, $\ln(\rho_tM^*_{it}/P_tY_{it})$.] To relate it to the materials condition (@eq-share-net), which holds for true materials, I subtract and add the log share of true materials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_{it} &= \ln\left(\frac{(1-\tau_P)\rho_t M^*_{it}}{(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}}\right)-\ln\left(\frac{(1-\tau_P)\rho_t M_{it}}{(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}}\right)+\ln\left(\frac{(1-\tau_P)\rho_t M_{it}}{(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}}\right)\\
&= \ln\left(\frac{M^*_{it}}{M_{it}}\right)+\ln\beta-\varepsilon_{it}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last line uses @eq-share-net to replace the log share of true materials. The remaining term is the log ratio of reported to true materials. Let $u_{it}\equiv\ln(M^*_{it}/M_{it})=\ln(1+e_{it}/M_{it})$ denote this log overreporting ratio. Then

$$
s_{it}=\ln\beta-\varepsilon_{it}+u_{it}.
$$ {#eq-foc-cd}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note (outline): why $u$, a ratio, and not the level $e$** (slides `700-deconvolving-evasion.qmd`, "I don't need $f_e$, actually"):

- Under Cobb-Douglas the firm's true materials are a share of revenue, so the wedge between $M^*$ and $M$ enters $\mathcal V$ only as $\ln(M^*/M)$, never as the level $e$.
- A ratio is adjusted for the firm's true input level, so it is comparable across firms of different sizes; a level $e$ would need normalizing anyway.
- @sec-deconvolution reports the overreporting ratio $e/M=\exp(u)-1$ directly.

:::

## Identifying the output elasticity of materials {#sec-testing-beta}

<!-- Dropped (Hans, 2026-10-10: no generality framing; Assumption 1 stated for corporations). Was:

**Assumption 1 (Non-evaders).** Corporations do not overreport inputs (@sec-setting-jo).

For corporations, $u_{it}=0$, and @eq-foc-cd becomes $s_{it}=\ln\beta-\varepsilon_{it}$.

In addition, I impose the following assumption.

**Assumption 2 (Independence).** The measurement error in output, $\varepsilon_{it}$, is independent of overreporting $u_{it}$, of true materials $M_{it}$, and of the firm's juridical organization, with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{it}]=0$.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note:** the approved paper states this as a timing assumption on an output shock ("firms choose overreporting before the output shock", citing @Gandhi2020, @Ackerberg2021, @Ackerberg2019). Following the supervisors, $\varepsilon$ is measurement error in output, not an output shock [@Gandhi2020], so independence is the classical measurement-error assumption and productivity is $\exp(\omega)$, not $\exp(\omega+\varepsilon)$. One sentence on why measurement error, and a contrast with GNR, belongs here or in @sec-model.

:::

Taking expectations among corporations recovers the output elasticity of materials, because measurement error has mean zero and is independent of juridical organization (Assumption 2):

$$
    \ln\beta=\mathbb{E}\left[s_{it}\mid \text{corporation}\right].
$$ {#eq-foc-cd-exp}

With $\ln\beta$ known, the corporations' share also recovers their measurement error, $\varepsilon_{it}=\ln\beta-s_{it}$, and with it its distribution, $f_\varepsilon$.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

## The observed residual {#sec-testing-residual}

Having recovered the output elasticity of materials, $\beta$, I can form the following variable from observed data for every firm. Subtracting $\ln\beta$ from both sides of @eq-foc-cd gives

$$
\mathcal V_{it}\equiv s_{it}-\ln\beta=u_{it}-\varepsilon_{it}.
$$ {#eq-ob-ev}

The observed residual recovers overreporting up to measurement error, which is independent of overreporting. Among unincorporated firms, its expected value is the expected overreporting, $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal V_{it}\mid\text{unincorporated}]=\mathbb{E}[u_{it}\mid\text{unincorporated}]$, because measurement error has mean zero in every juridical organization (Assumption 2). Since firms never underreport ($e_{it}\ge0$, @sec-model), $u_{it}\ge0$, and this expected value is zero only if no unincorporated firm overreports.

## Testing for overreporting {#sec-testing-test}

@eq-ob-ev suggests a test for overreporting. Let $\mu_{\mathcal V}\equiv\mathbb{E}[\mathcal V_{it}\mid\text{unincorporated}]$. The null hypothesis is that unincorporated firms do not overreport, $H_0:\mu_{\mathcal V}=0$, and the alternative is that they do, $H_1:\mu_{\mathcal V}>0$. The test is one-sided because no firm has an incentive to underreport deductible inputs. Underreporting would raise a firm's tax liability and decrease after-tax profits (@sec-model). A rejection can therefore only point to overreporting.

To test the null hypothesis, I build a confidence set for $\mu_{\mathcal V}$ by test inversion. The test detects overreporting where the confidence set is non-empty and excludes zero. Test inversion consists of testing every candidate value $\mu_0$ on a grid over $[0,1]$ and keeping the values the test does not reject. These values form a confidence set for $\mu_{\mathcal V}$. Inverting a test at the 5 percent level gives a 95 percent confidence set [@CasellaBerger2002, sec. 9.2.1].

The test described above implicitly takes $\beta$ from corporations as the true parameter. I make the assumption explicit by using two moments, one for each group. Let $C_{it}$ equal one for corporations and zero otherwise. If $\beta$ is the output elasticity of materials and $\mu_0\ge0$ is the expected residual of unincorporated firms,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[C_{it}(s_{it}-\ln\beta)\big]=0,\qquad \mathbb{E}\big[(1-C_{it})(s_{it}-\ln\beta-\mu_0)\big]=0.
$$ {#eq-test-moments}

The first moment restates @eq-foc-cd-exp; the second states that the residual of unincorporated firms (@eq-ob-ev) has mean $\mu_0\in[0,1]$.

Let $\hat g(\ln\beta,\mu_0)$ stack the sample means of the two moments over the $n$ firm-years of the industry. The test statistic is

$$
TS(\ln\beta,\mu_0)=n\,\hat g(\ln\beta,\mu_0)'\,\hat\Omega(\ln\beta,\mu_0)^{-1}\,\hat g(\ln\beta,\mu_0),
$$

where $\hat\Omega$ is the covariance matrix of the moments, clustered by plant and re-estimated at each candidate rather than fixed at a preliminary estimate [@AndersonRubin1949; @StockWright2000]. Under the null hypothesis, the statistic is asymptotically chi-squared with $d_g$ degrees of freedom.[^dg-df]

[^dg-df]: I evaluate the statistic at $\ln\hat\beta$, the corporations' mean log share. That is, I take the corporations' estimate as the true value. The first moment is exactly zero at this value, and the statistic tests only the second: whether the residual of unincorporated firms has mean $\mu_0$. Hence $d_g=1$. @sec-app-test-robustness reports a conservative version of the test with $d_g=2$, and an alternative bootstrap test that carries the sampling error of $\ln\hat\beta$.

<!-- Already established: 
For each industry, @tbl-evasion-test displays the estimated mean of $\mathcal V_{it}$ among unincorporated firms and the values of $\mu_{\mathcal V}$ in $[0,1]$ that the test does not reject at the 5 percent level.  -->

The test does not depend on the functional forms of the detection probability and the cost of evasion, nor on the Cobb-Douglas form of the technology. A truthful firm faces no detection and incurs no cost of evasion, $q(0,\cdot)=0$ and $\kappa(0,\cdot)=0$; under the null hypothesis, every firm's materials condition is therefore the one without evasion. For any technology that corporations and unincorporated firms share, the residual is then $-\varepsilon_{it}$ under the null, and under the alternative its expected value is positive as long as output is concave in materials. With a second flexible input that is not deductible, a monotone output elasticity of that input replaces concavity, but the sign of the residual under the alternative is then not known in advance. @sec-app-test-robustness derives both results.

**Draft note (outline for the test design and results; replaces the old results paragraphs of `200-deconv.qmd`, whose industry counts come from an earlier table):**

- Design (2026-09-26, replaces the bootstrap): test inversion over $\mu_{\mathcal V}\in[0,1]$, with $\ln\hat\beta$ from corporations taken as the true value; moments (corporations: $s-\ln\hat D$; unincorporated firms: $s-\ln\hat D-\mu$), plant-clustered, centred covariance re-estimated at each candidate; sharp $\chi^2_1$ (the corporations' moment holds exactly at $\ln\hat D$), conservative $\chi^2_2$. Sample: log materials share net of sales taxes, juridical organization codes 6--9 excluded. The earlier bootstrap overstated significance: its resampling joined sampled plants back by plant only, so plants that switch legal form brought rows from the other group and the replicates were not centred on the estimate. The corrected bootstrap and the conservative test are in @sec-app-test-robustness.

:::

## Results {#sec-testing-results}

I test for overreporting the 20 largest manufacturing industries by the number of firm-years.

The test detects overreporting in 9 of the 18 industries liable for the sales tax (@tbl-evasion-test): Beverages (313)[^bevs], Textiles (321), Wearing apparel (322), Footwear (324), Wood products (331), Printing and publishing (342), Non-metallic minerals (369) and, narrowly, Industrial chemicals (351) and Other chemicals (352). In the first seven, the test also rejects at the 1 percent level. The nine industries include 4 of the 5 largest by output and together produce 41 percent of manufacturing output.[^unlk]

[^bevs]: In Beverages (313), the mean residual of unincorporated firms, 0.39, is the largest of any tested industry. It partly reflects differences in products between the two groups. Corporations produce mostly beer and soft drinks; unincorporated firms produce wine, spirits and soft drinks. Beer corporations report a low materials share, which lowers the benchmark. Within the same product (four-digit industry), the mean residual falls to 0.23 but remains positive. The mean is also higher because the sample excludes state enterprises (@sec-setting-jo). In this industry they are distilleries, and the departments held a monopoly on producing aguardiente and rum [@Ocampo1983, pp. 251--254]. Their materials share is lower than the corporations'. With them and the other excluded organizations in the sample, the mean residual is 0.23, and the test still rejects correct reporting at the 1 percent level.

[^unlk]: The rejections are unlikely to come from testing many industries. If no industry overreported, a test at the 5 percent level across the 20 industries would reject in about one of them by chance, and the probability of nine or more rejections would be about $2\times10^{-7}$.

The test does not detect overreporting in either industry exempt from the sales tax, Food products (311) and Other food products (312). This is expected. Firms in these industries had no incentives to evade sales taxes (@sec-setting-incentive). The result aligns with the model, which predicts little overreporting where the reward is small.

In the other nine liable industries, the test fails to reject correct reporting. The confidence set either does not exclude zero or is empty, no candidate in $[0,1]$ is accepted. As with any statistical test, a failure to reject is inconclusive.
